summary: A composite monarchy and overseas colonial system connecting American, European, African and Asian territories through conquest, settlement and regulated trade.
capital: Madrid from 1561; the royal court moved to Valladolid in 1601–1606.
currency: Silver peso of eight reales was a major international trade coin; other currencies varied by territory and period.
economy: American silver, export agriculture and regulated shipping sustained imperial revenues; forced labor and slavery were integral to colonial production.
military: Armed Atlantic convoys protected bullion shipments; colonial conquest depended on Spanish forces and Indigenous allies.
contributions: Transatlantic and transpacific routes connected world trade; colonial rule also caused dispossession, coerced labor and profound demographic loss.
origin: Crown-sponsored Atlantic voyages and conquest established American colonies, followed by expansion across the Pacific.
decline: American independence movements dismantled most mainland rule; later decolonization reduced overseas possessions, including Spain’s withdrawal from Western Sahara in 1976.
periodNote: 1492–1976 is an overseas-imperial convention. The final date marks Spain’s withdrawal from Western Sahara, whose status remained unresolved; it is not a universal endpoint for all Spanish overseas possessions.
